title: Winning bids without underpricing
audience: Owners of small Australian property trade businesses who respond to bid requests from platforms, agents and direct enquiries
learningOutcomes: Reply to a bid request with a personalised message that names the client's job and proposes a clear next step.
Prepare an accurate estimate for a site visit or a remote quote, with inclusions, exclusions and assumptions stated.
Avoid underpricing by checking every bid against the estimate and the hourly rate or minimum charge.

instruction.heading: The first reply shapes the next step
instruction.body: A bid request is often one of several a client receives. The first reply should show that the request was read. Use the client's name, refer to the job by its details, and say what happens next, such as a call, a site visit or a written quote by a set date. Speed matters, because a prompt reply signals that the business will be responsive on the job. Where a platform shows the client's phone number with the request, a call to discuss the job is a normal reply to it. Avoid a generic template sent to every request, because clients notice when a message does not match their question.

instruction.heading: Offering a site visit when the scope is unclear
instruction.body: A bid made from a photo or a short description can be wrong. Offer a site visit when the job involves access problems, hidden conditions or more than one service type. Bring a portfolio of the owner's own work, the service list and the estimate form. A visit also shows the client how the business works. Record what was seen, what the client asked for and what the client did not ask for, so the scope can be confirmed in writing.

instruction.heading: Pricing from the estimate, not from competitors
instruction.body: Cutting a price to win one job can leave the business with a loss it cannot recover. Build the price from the estimate (“Estimating a job from labour, materials and extras”) and from the hourly rate or minimum charge (“Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge”). If the scope is not yet clear, state the assumptions and what would change the price, rather than guessing low. Competitor prices are a guide, not a target, and a comparison is only useful with businesses whose insurance, licences and costs are similar. Some estimating guides add a 10 to 20 percent allowance to estimates for unexpected work; if the owner uses one, state it as an assumption. Keep the quote valid for a stated period. Tell the client what is included, what is excluded and what would need a variation. If a warranty or guarantee is offered, state its terms clearly. Under the Australian Consumer Law, services must be carried out with due care and skill, be fit for the purpose stated, and be supplied within a reasonable time where no timeframe is agreed, as the business.gov.au guide sets out. Check the current rules before writing any warranty wording.

instruction.heading: Asking for references and reviews
instruction.body: Clients who trust the business are more likely to hire it. Offer references where the client has agreed to share them. Ask each client for a review after the job, and include the review link in the next message where the platform allows it. Keep the reviews on file with their date and the client's permission to use them.

procedure: Read the request in full, and note the scope, the access, the timing and any hazards.
Reply within the response time the business has set, using the client's name and the job details.
Offer a site visit where the scope or access is unclear, and record what was seen and asked.
Build the price from the estimate and from the hourly rate or minimum charge.
Write the quote with inclusions, exclusions, assumptions, the validity period and the variation terms.
Follow up at a set time, and request a review once the job is complete.

workedExamples.situation: Two businesses bid on the same job. One bids well below the estimate with no stated exclusions. The other bids at the estimate, lists the access conditions and offers a site visit.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which bid should the owner send, and why?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner should send a bid that matches the estimate and states the access conditions, because the lower bid cannot be delivered at that price without a loss or a later variation. Stating the access, the working height and the exclusions protects both parties. If the work at height is outside the owner's permitted scope, the owner must check the safe work rules in “Ladders, elevated access and fall prevention” before bidding, or refer the work.

equipmentAndPpe: Bid response template with spaces for the client's name and job details
Site visit checklist and estimate form
Quote template with inclusions, exclusions and validity

commonErrors.error: Sending the same generic bid to every request.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the client's name and the job details in every first reply.

commonErrors.error: Underpricing to win the job, then asking for more money later.
commonErrors.prevention: Price from the estimate, state the assumptions, and put any variation in writing.

commonErrors.error: Promising a warranty or result the business cannot deliver.
commonErrors.prevention: State the warranty terms, check the consumer guarantee position, and promise only what can be delivered.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Check them with the ACCC or a legal adviser before using any warranty wording.

Work at height, electrical work, gas work and other work that carries licence or safety limits must be bid only within what the owner is permitted to do, or the work must be referred (see “Ladders, elevated access and fall prevention”, “Electrical boundaries and referral” and “Water, plumbing and gas boundaries”). Licence rules for electrical and gas work differ between states and territories, so check the rules where the work is done. This lesson grants no licence.

qualityStandard: Each bid names the client and the job details, and states the next step.
Each quote lists inclusions, exclusions, assumptions, the validity period and the variation terms.
No bid is below the estimate without a recorded reason and a check of the scope.
documentationEvidence: Bid log with the date, reply time, job details and outcome
Site visit notes recording what was seen and what was asked
Written quote with inclusions, exclusions and validity
summary: Reply with specific details and a clear next step.
Price from the estimate, not from the fear of losing the job.
State exclusions and variations in writing, and ask for reviews.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best first reply to a bid request?
options: A generic template sent to every job with the same wording every time, sent by email
A reply that uses the client's name, refers to the job and proposes a clear next step
A low price with no details and no date for a follow-up or a site visit
No reply until the job is booked and then a reply with the price only

knowledgeChecks.question: A bid is far below the estimate, with no exclusions stated. What is the main risk?
options: The client will be impressed by the price and will expect the same price for every job
The business may be unable to deliver at that price, and a later variation will be needed
The insurance premium will fall and the bank fees and the rent will fall too
The business will need a larger van for every job it takes

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a quote state its exclusions and assumptions?
options: So the owner can avoid writing a quote for the job at all
So both parties know what is included and what would need a variation
So the price can be raised without notice and the work can be changed
So the client cannot ask questions about the work at all

officialReferences.title: Australian Consumer Law and your business (business.gov.au)
officialReferences.covers: business.gov.au (page dated 27 May 2025): services must be carried out with due care and skill, be fit for the purpose stated, and be supplied within a reasonable time if no timeframe is agreed. The page says businesses must give customers truthful information about their goods and services. It does not mention quotes or estimates; the rules on quotes and advertising claims remain UNCONFIRMED. Publisher: business.gov.au.

officialReferences.title: Prepare quotes (business.gov.au)
officialReferences.covers: business.gov.au page (dated 01 August 2025): if a customer accepts a quote it becomes a legally binding contract, and a good quote is clear, specific and complete. The page recommends writing the quote down and lists items such as business details and ABN, a work description, itemised costs, GST where applicable, payment terms, start and finish dates and an expiry date. It does not mention estimates or rules for particular services. Publisher: business.gov.au.
